Stopped reading there. Expecting a finished product when it is released is in no way entitled.

If you bought a new car and had it delivered to your house and they unloaded a frame and a crate full of parts and told you they'd have to assemble it on site and it would take 2 days, you'd be pissed as hell, and rightly so, because you ordered a complete and assembled car. The same thing applies when you buy a game. You're not paying $60+ for an unfinished product, and god forbid you're one of the countless people with poor or no internet access or data caps, then you might not be receiving the patch at all, which means you will likely never experience the finished product you paid for. And don't give me that shit about "the process" because games have been around for over 50 fucking years and the "process" is pretty much the same, but day-one patches are just now becoming a widespread thing. If anything, the job has gotten even easier since everybody just re-uses assets from other games and builds on engines that have been around for a decade. I can excuse a day-one patch for a game like No Man's Sky that is being made by like six people and has had a pretty rough ride up to release with floods and other bullshit, but this sympathy does not extend to people like EA cranking out the same games they have been for 10 years who all of a sudden are more worried about farting out a game as fast as they can than making sure it's actually finished.

Personally, I'm not that assblasted about it because I'm lucky enough to have good internet and no data caps and while it is annoying to have to wait 5-30 minutes for a patch to download when I get a new game, I'm not enraged by it or anything. But trying to say I would be entitled if I was upset is absolutely bullshit. Whatever excuse you want to make for day-one patches is fine, but at the end of the day it always boils down to a company not shipping a finished product. It doesn't matter the reason.
